thread.title: 10 Issues Preventing A Bull Rally - Cramer's Mad Money (11/19/18)

author: SA Editor Mohit Manghnani
title: 10 Issues Preventing A Bull Rally - Cramer's Mad Money (11/19/18)
text:
Stocks discussed on the in-depth session of Jim Cramer's Mad Money TV Program, Monday , November 19.
The market selloff keeps continuing, and investors have questions. "When does this rout end? When do the buyers come in? When do the sellers finish? Frankly, we don't know, and that uncertainty is what allows this roving bear market to keep tearing us to pieces," the Mad Money host said. There are ten issues that need to be fixed before the market can bounce back.
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ): The market cannot stabilize unless Apple stabilizes. While the technical indicators suggest that selloff is over, the stock hasn't found a bottom yet. "My view? Apple is a long-term hold, with its huge installed base giving the company's service revenue stream a lot of room to grow, which is why you own it and don't trade it," said Cramer. The stock will not bottom unless it sees more analyst downgrades. Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ): The stock has turned into a disaster. "Mark Zuckerberg, the CEO, is now making Elon Musk look like the Dalai Lama. I've been calling for some sort of elder statesman to come in, like when Eric Schmidt took the reins at Google in 2001, giving the founders some adult supervision and putting the company on better footing. That's what Facebook desperately needs right now," Cramer opined. The software stocks have to stop going down. "The incredible thing is there's no concrete evidence whatsoever that anything is really wrong. Nobody's seen a real slowdown in the web. How does it end? These brutal declines in tech typically end when the longs are finished selling and the valuations can be sustained. We're not there yet," Cramer noted. Buying on dips: Cramer is not seeing enough buying on market dips. Unless that doesn't happen, the market cannot find its footing. China: The trade war issue with China needs to be fixed. "If this administration views trade with the People's Republic as simply providing fuel for their attempts to become a superpower, you could easily imagine them cutting off that trade entirely," said Cramer. This is bad for American companies. Fed: The Fed needs to change their stance on three rate hikes in 2019 and be data-dependent. "The Fed wants concrete evidence of people being thrown out of work before they become less hawkish. I do not think that's the way to run the Fed, but I am definitively not in charge," Cramer said. There is confusion in the market, with defensive stocks going up. "Given that nobody thinks you can slip into a recession so fast after such strong economic numbers, there's genuine confusion. Confusion makes people want to sell," he added. The technical trend for stocks still looks ugly. Retail: The retail stocks are going down. It's clear that the economy cannot handle rate hikes, as even the good retailer stocks are falling. Selling: The market is not in oversold territory yet. "A bounce could still be long in the tooth. The good news? If we keep falling at this pace, it won't be long before we reach oversold levels, where all hope is extinguished and we can bounce," he said. "I've been highlighting these issues for what feels like ages. There's always some new people watching, though. These have only grown more acute with time, which is why we could be headed lower, even if we get a snapback rally from an oversold position," Cramer concluded.
Bad timing The market seems to be in a bear phase, and any good news is also discounted. It's just the timing of the market and nothing more. The good companies that came public are going down with the rest of the market. For instance, the outdoor equipment and gear maker Yeti Holdings (NYSE: YETI ) came public three weeks ago and no one noticed.
Its revenue has seen high growth from $90 million in 2013 to $640 million last year, and yet, the company is trading below its IPO price. Cramer likes the company, but its balance sheet has $390 million of private equity-backed debt, and he is not a fan of deals when private equity still has a controlling interest in a company. Still, it is trading at an attractive multiple considering its growth rate.
Molson Coors (NYSE: TAP ) Molson had been falling out of favor since 2016 with the consumer shift from mass market beers to craft beers. Since then, the stock has lost half its value.
However, in the company's Q3 report , it surprised the market with good performance and positive guidance. Looking at other brands, it is clear that domestic beer will not recover. "Now, the beer business hasn't suddenly turned around, and let's not say that it has. Molson Coors still saw a 1% decline in worldwide brand volume, with real weakness in North America. The bear thesis remains the same: maybe Molson Coors has become a better operator, but the fact remains that their core U.S. beer business is in trouble," added Cramer.
However, international sales remain strong and the company is cutting costs. It is also investing in the Canadian cannabis market, which could be as big as $10 billion a year, and cannabis-based beverages could account for 20-30% of the total volume.
"Molson Coors is definitely getting its act together, but I want to see some signs of real improvement in the core business before I recommend this stock as an investment. But if you want to buy Molson Coors purely on speculation that the thing has really turned around? Well, as long as you're prepared to lose a little money, be my guest," Cramer concluded.
CEO interview - Boot Barn (NASDAQ: BOOT ) Boot Barn reported a good quarter . Cramer interviewed CEO Jim Conroy to know what to expect for the holiday season.
Conroy said business at the company should not be drastically affected by tariffs on Chinese goods, as it imports only 7-8% of the private-label brands from China. Its third-party manufacturers are seeking alternative manufacturing sources. "China has a compelling position in the trade landscape. Things are manufactured there for a reason, and I think their productivity is strong. My personal view is they'll figure out a way to continue to be an importer to the U.S," he noted.
A large portion of the company's stores are located in Texas, and the oil prices haven't affected it much. "I think the exposure to oil for Boot Barn is a little bit overblown. If we went back for the last eight years, our same-store sales have comped, on average, 8%, and that includes a precipitous decline in oil," the CEO explained.
The company is planning to double its store count from the existing 233 stores in the coming years.
Viewer calls taken by Cramer Boise Cascade (NYSE: BCC ): It doesn't deserve to be this low, and Cramer wants the Fed to take notice.
Aurora Cannabis (NYSE: ACB ): It's a highly speculative stock.
